steps.do: Display the contents of the module definition file.
Display the contents of the module checksum file.
Compare the file sizes to verify presence.

K-024084.example: The model runs cat go.mod and cat go.sum to visually inspect the dependency list and checksums.
K-024084.check: Both files exist and contain valid dependency entries.
traps: Ignoring go.sum changes can lead to build failures.
Not checking go.mod misses new dependencies.
Assuming files are updated without visual verification.

steps.do: Check for differences in module definition file.
Check for differences in module checksum file.
Report the exit status of the last diff check.

K-024085.example: The model runs git diff --exit-code on go.mod and go.sum. If both return 0, the files match the last commit.
K-024085.check: git diff --exit-code returns 0 for both files.
traps: Skipping the check leaves stale dependencies.
Ignoring the exit code of git diff misses file changes.
Not checking both go.mod and go.sum.

steps.do: Run the unchanged baseline five times to capture the spread.
Calculate the standard deviation of the resulting metrics.
Record the mean and standard deviation for later comparison.

K-024137.example: Running the baseline five times yields times of 102, 105, 98, 101, 103 ms. The standard deviation is 2.2 ms.
K-024137.check: The output shows five distinct run results and a calculated standard deviation value.
traps: Using only one run to estimate noise.
Ignoring the standard deviation and looking only at the mean.
Running the modified version before stabilizing the baseline.

steps.do: Run the benchmark gate comparing build A and build B.
Check if the delta is within two standard errors.
If inconclusive, calculate how many more runs are needed.

K-024138.example: The gate reports a delta of 5 ms with a standard error of 2 ms. Since 5 is greater than 4 (2*2), it is outside the noise band.
K-024138.check: The gate output explicitly states whether the delta is noise, inconclusive, or a win/loss.
traps: Treating any positive delta as a win without checking the noise band.
Stopping the analysis immediately when the result is inconclusive.
Forgetting to compare against the calculated standard error.

steps.do: Generate pairs of data drawn from the same distribution.
Run the gate on the simulated pairs.
Count how often the gate calls pairs noise.

K-024139.example: Simulating 100 identical pairs, the gate calls 95 of them noise. This matches the expected 95% confidence level.
K-024139.check: The simulation report shows the call rate matches the theoretical probability for the chosen band.
traps: Using real data to validate the gate's statistical assumptions.
Not checking the false positive rate (calling noise a win).
Assuming the band is correct without calibration.

steps.do: Set the token and time caps for both sides.
Fix the random seed set for reproducibility.
Verify the configuration applies to both A and B.

K-024140.example: Both builds are configured with a 5000 token limit and 60-second timeout using seed 42. The config show command confirms these values.
K-024140.check: The config show output lists identical limits and seeds for both compared entities.
traps: Allowing one side to run to completion while the other hits a cap.
Using different random seeds for the two sides.
Forgetting to reset time limits between runs.

steps.do: Record wall time for each solved case.
Log the system load during the run.
Calculate success rate alongside wall time.

K-024141.example: The average wall time is 1.2 seconds with a 90% success rate. System load was logged at 75% average CPU usage.
K-024141.check: The output includes wall time, success rate, and a note on system load.
traps: Using CPU time instead of wall time for user-facing metrics.
Ignoring system load when interpreting wall time results.
Reporting only average time without success rate.

steps.do: Create a variant with component X removed.
Run the benchmark on the ablated variant.
Compare the ablated variant against the original bundle.

K-024142.example: Removing component X causes the time to increase by 20 ms. This indicates component X contributes to the performance gain.
K-024142.check: The compare output shows a specific metric change attributable to the removed component.
traps: Removing multiple components at once.
Assuming the whole bundle is responsible without testing parts.
Not keeping raw runs for the ablated versions.

steps.do: Extract file paths from the current plan draft.
Check if any listed files actually exist in the repository.
Identify missing files or incorrect paths in the plan.

Save the updated plan with risk annotations.

K-024566.check: Every file path in the plan exists or has a corresponding creation step in the plan.

Listing high-level risks instead of specific, actionable mitigation steps.
Forgetting to rename the file after updating, causing data loss.

steps.do: Check if the plan file starts with a correct title header.
Verify the presence of the Requirements section.
Count the number of implementation steps defined.
Confirm the file is not empty.
Report any missing sections to the user.

K-024567.example: If head -n 1 plan.md returns '# Implementation Plan', the title is correct. If grep finds no Requirements section, the check fails.
K-024567.check: All required headers are present and the step count is greater than zero.
traps: Using case-sensitive grep when headers might vary in capitalization.
Counting steps incorrectly if the formatting is inconsistent.
Failing to check if the file exists before reading it.

steps.do: List the key components involved in the feature.
Identify the specific functions or classes to modify.
Define the exact action for each component modification.
Order the steps by dependency hierarchy.
Write the detailed step list to a new file.

K-024568.example: For a payment feature, the tree command shows src/payments/ exists. The plan lists modifying PaymentService.ts before updating the API route.
K-024568.check: The detailed_steps.md file contains numbered steps with specific file paths and actions.
traps: Creating steps that are too vague, like 'update code', without specifying which function.
Ordering steps without considering which files depend on which others.
Skipping the tree or grep step, leading to a plan based on guesswork.

steps.do: Read the current plan steps.
Identify steps involving database changes or external APIs.
Assign a high complexity flag to identified steps.
Reorder steps to prioritize high-complexity items first.
Save the plan with complexity annotations.

K-024569.example: Steps mentioning 'psql' are marked as high complexity. The plan moves the database migration step to the top of the list.
K-024569.check: High-complexity steps appear before low-complexity steps in the final plan.
traps: Marking all steps as high complexity, which loses priority distinctions.
Failing to reorder the steps after assigning complexity labels.
Overlooking external API calls that are often high-risk but not obvious.

steps.do: Extract the feature name from the title.
List the main components affected by the change.
Synthesize the purpose and scope into a short paragraph.
Prepend the summary to the plan file.
Replace the original plan with the updated version.

K-024570.example: The feature name is 'Login'. The components are src/auth.ts and src/api.ts. The summary states: 'This plan updates auth logic and API routes for user login.'
K-024570.check: The plan.md file starts with a clear Overview section summarizing the feature.
traps: Writing a summary that is too long, exceeding the 3-sentence limit.
Using generic words like 'some files' instead of specific component names.
Failing to move the temp file back, leaving the plan unchanged.

steps.do: Write the question ending with a question mark.
State the deadline date for the decision.
Identify who has final approval authority.
Save the question text to a note file.

K-024627.example: For a migration task, the question is 'Do we move to Postgres 16 by Friday?' The approver is the team lead and the date command outputs 'Fri 10:00'.
K-024627.check: The text ends with '?' and contains a specific date and name.
traps: Using a vague statement instead of a question.
Forgetting to assign a specific person to approve.
Including implementation details in the question.

steps.do: Write factual constraints with their source URLs.
Write assumptions that need verification.
Check if the source URL is valid.
List the distinct constraints using a tool.

K-024628.example: A constraint is 'API limit is 100 req/min (docs.io/limits)' and an assumption is 'Latency is stable'. The curl command returns 200 OK for the docs link.
K-024628.check: Facts have sources, assumptions do not, and distinct lines are sorted.
traps: Mixing guesses into the facts list.
Citing outdated documentation without checking the date.
Forgetting to verify the source link works.

steps.do: Define criteria: build cost, reverse cost, risk, fit.
Assign a score from 1 to 5 for each option.
Verify scores are integers using a filter.
Sort options by total score.

traps: Using adjectives like 'good' instead of numbers.
Changing criteria after seeing the scores.
Forgetting to include the 'fit' criterion.

steps.do: Write the chosen option and one-paragraph reason.
Define a measurable revisit trigger condition.
Log the decision using the sampo command.
Verify the log entry exists.

K-024630.example: Choose 'Postgres'. Reason: 'Better fit for concurrent users'. Trigger: 'p95 latency > 200ms'. The sampo command outputs 'Decision logged: Postgres'.
K-024630.check: The sampo command succeeds and the trigger is measurable.

Forgetting to mention what was rejected.
Not linking the decision to the task brief.

steps.do: Check if the question mark is present.
Check if three options are listed.
Check if the revisit trigger is defined.

Having only two options instead of three.
Omitting the revisit trigger section.

steps.do: Change to the project root directory
Run npm audit filtered for high severity issues
Review the output for listed vulnerable packages

steps.do: Search for common secret patterns like API_KEY or SECRET
Filter results to ignore test files and mocks
Inspect the matched lines for actual values

Matching variables named `apiKey` that are read from environment variables safely.

Check if user variables are interpolated directly into strings
Confirm use of parameterized queries or safe ORMs

K-024943.check: The output shows lines where user input is concatenated with SQL strings, revealing unsafe patterns.
traps: Assuming all ORM usage is safe without checking for raw query methods.
Missing dynamic table names that are not sanitized.
Confusing template literals for string interpolation in older JS versions.
Ignoring stored procedure calls that might bypass validation.

steps.do: Identify in-scope patterns like SSRF, SQLi, or command injection that affect remote users.
List repository files to understand the project structure and entry points.
Search for user-controlled inputs passed to dangerous functions like eval or exec.
Check for SQL injection vectors in query builder usage.

K-025303.example: The repo is a Python web app. I used find to locate main.py. I searched for eval usage in request handlers to find potential RCE vectors.
K-025303.check: The grep commands return specific lines where user input is passed directly to dangerous functions, indicating a potential vulnerability.
traps: Do not report local-only issues like pickle.loads without network reachability.
Ignore theoretical vulnerabilities that cannot be triggered remotely.
Do not include low-signal findings like informational leaks.
Focus on patterns that clearly allow unauthorized access or execution.

steps.do: Look for URL fetching functions that accept user-supplied URLs.
Check if the code validates the URL protocol to prevent http/https schemes.
Verify if the code resolves the IP address before making the request.

K-025304.example: I found a Flask route accepting a 'url' parameter. I checked if the code used socket.gethostbyname to validate it against localhost IPs.
K-025304.check: The grep results show whether the code explicitly validates the destination IP or protocol, confirming if SSRF is mitigated.
traps: Do not assume all URL fetching is vulnerable; check for validation logic.
Ignore internal APIs that are not remotely accessible.
Do not confuse SSRF with simple open redirects.
Focus on the data flow from user input to the network request.

steps.do: Search for string concatenation or formatting in SQL queries.
Check for parameterized query usage to ensure safe database interaction.
Verify that input sanitization is applied before query construction.

K-025305.example: I scanned a Node.js Express app for string interpolation in Sequelize calls. I confirmed that parameterized queries were used consistently in the found lines.
K-025305.check: The grep results show queries using placeholders (?) or named parameters, indicating protection against SQL injection.
traps: Do not report ORM methods that automatically parameterize queries.
Ignore local database operations if remote access is impossible.
Do not mistake variable assignment for query execution.
Focus on the final SQL string construction.

steps.do: Search for system call functions like os.system or exec.Command.
Check if user input is passed directly to these commands without validation.
Look for shell=True usage which increases injection risk.

K-025306.example: I found a Python script passing user input to os.system. I verified that the input was not sanitized and shell=True was used.
K-025306.check: The grep results highlight lines where user input flows directly into command execution, confirming an injection vector.
traps: Do not report hardcoded command lines with no user input.
Ignore subprocess calls that use lists instead of strings.
Do not confuse logging statements with command execution.
Focus on the direct link between user input and system command.

steps.do: Search for file open operations that use user-supplied paths.
Check if the code resolves the path and checks for traversal sequences.
Verify that the resolved path is within the intended directory.

K-025307.example: I reviewed a static file server. I checked if the code used os.path.abspath and verified the path was within the static directory.
K-025307.check: The grep results show validation logic that ensures the requested file is within the allowed base directory.
traps: Do not report file reads that use hardcoded safe paths.
Ignore input that is strictly alphanumeric and cannot contain dots.
Do not confuse path display with path usage.
Focus on the actual file system access.

steps.do: Search for template syntax that renders user input without auto-escaping.
Check for manual rendering functions like innerHTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML.
Verify that content security policies or escaping filters are applied.

K-025308.example: I inspected a React component rendering user comments. I confirmed that dangerouslySetInnerHTML was used but passed through a sanitizer function.
K-025308.check: The grep results indicate whether raw HTML is inserted directly or passed through a sanitization function.
traps: Do not report server-side rendered HTML if the framework auto-escapes by default.
Ignore static text content that cannot be modified by users.
Do not confuse CSS variables with script injection.
Focus on the binding of user data to HTML content.
